A '''canonical basis''' (or '''standard basis''') is a [[vector space basis]] conventionally determined by the definition of a given [[vector space]] for convenience.

== [[Coordinate space]] $\mathbb{F}^n$ ==

'''Canonical basis'''

$$
B_\text{Canonical}=\{\vec e_1,\cdot, \vec e_n\},
$$

where

$$
\vec{e}_1=(1,0,\dots,0),\quad
\vec{e}_2=(0,1,0,\dots,0),\quad \dots,\quad
\vec{e}_n=(0,\dots,0,1).
$$

Every vector $\vec{x}=(x_1,\dots,x_n)\in \mathbb{F}^n$ is written uniquely as

$$
\forall \vec x \in \mathbb{F}^n: \vec{x}=(x_1,\dots,x_n)=x_1\vec{e}_1+\cdots+x_n\vec{e}_n.
$$

== [[Polynomial]]s of degree $\le n$ ==

'''Canonical basis'''

$$
B=\{1,x,x^2,\dots,x^n\}.
$$

== $m\times n$ Matrix ==

$$
B=\{\mathbf{E}_{ij}|i \in \{1,\cdots,m\}, j \in \{1,\cdots,n\}\},
$$

where

$$
\forall \mathbb{E}_{ij}=(e_{xy}): \\
\exists! x_1,y_1
\begin{cases}
e_{xy}=1,& x=x_1,y=y_1\\
e_{xy}=0,& \text{elsewise}.
\end{cases}
$$
